State-dependent local projections (Auerbach-Gorodnichenko)

Source: R/lp-state.R
lp_state.Rd

Local projections whose coefficients depend on the state of the economy through a transition function of a switching variable \(z\). For each horizon \(h\), $$y_{t+h} = F(z_{t-1})\,[\alpha^L_h + \beta^L_h s_t + \gamma^{L\prime}_h w_t] + (1-F(z_{t-1}))\,[\alpha^H_h + \beta^H_h s_t + \gamma^{H\prime}_h w_t] + e_{t+h},$$ with the smooth logistic transition \(F(z) = 1/(1+\exp\{\gamma(\tilde z - c)\})\) on the standardised variable \(\tilde z=(z-\bar z)/\mathrm{sd}(z)\) (Auerbach & Gorodnichenko 2012, 2013; \(F\to1\) in the "low" state, e.g. recession when \(z\) is growth) or the binary version \(F = 1\{\tilde z_{t-1} < c\}\). The state enters lagged by one period to avoid contemporaneous feedback of the shock on the state. All \(2\times\) regressors are estimated in one regression per horizon (C++ engine), with Newey-West errors, and the cross-horizon covariance is used to test \(H_0:\beta^L_h=\beta^H_h\) pointwise (HAC t-test) and jointly across horizons (Wald).

Usage

lp_state(
  Y,
  shock,
  state,
  horizon = 12L,
  lags = 4L,
  contemp = NULL,
  controls = NULL,
  responses = NULL,
  cumulative = NULL,
  transition = c("logistic", "binary"),
  gamma = 1.5,
  cutoff = 0,
  low_share = NULL,
  hp_lambda = NULL,
  standardise = TRUE,
  timing = c("contemporaneous", "lagged"),
  lags_lin = lags,
  shock_type = 0L,
  state_const = TRUE,
  trend = FALSE,
  se = c("nw", "hc"),
  nw_lag = NULL,
  level = c(0.68, 0.9),
  dof_adjust = FALSE
)

Arguments

Y

data frame / tibble / matrix (T x K) of responses (and the source of lag controls). Non-numeric columns (e.g. a date) are dropped.

shock

the shock \(s_t\): a variable of Y (tidyselect; observed shock, unit-impact normalisation) or a numeric vector of length T (external shock series, e.g. narrative).

state

switching variable \(z\): a variable of Y (tidyselect, one variable) or a numeric vector of length T.

horizon

maximum horizon H.

lags

number of lags of Y in the controls (and of an external shock).

contemp

<tidy-select> variables of Y entered contemporaneously as controls. For a recursive (Cholesky) identification with shock a variable of Y, list the variables ordered before the shock.

controls

optional extra T x q matrix of controls.

responses

<tidy-select> responses to use (default all variables of Y).

cumulative

<tidy-select> variables whose response is cumulated (\(\sum_{j=0}^h y_{t+j}\)), for variables measured in differences.

transition

"logistic" (smooth) or "binary".

gamma

logistic smoothness (larger is closer to a regime switch).

cutoff

cutoff \(c\) on the standardised scale; ignored if low_share is given.

low_share

optional share in (0, 1) of observations to place below the cutoff (sets \(c\) to that quantile of \(\tilde z\)).

hp_lambda

if not NULL, use the Hodrick-Prescott cycle of state (smoothing parameter, e.g. 1600 for quarterly data) as switching variable.

standardise

standardise \(z\) (after filtering) to mean 0, sd 1.

timing

"contemporaneous" or "lagged" (the lpirfs convention), see Details.

lags_lin

lag length of the linear VAR used for the impact matrix (timing = "lagged").

shock_type

"lagged" only: 0 standard-deviation, 1 unit shock.

state_const

interact the constant with the state (state-specific intercepts); lpirfs uses a common constant, so set FALSE when comparing.

trend

"lagged" only: include a linear time trend (lpirfs trend = 1).

se

"nw" Newey-West/Bartlett or "hc" Eicker-Huber-White (HC1).

nw_lag

Newey-West truncation lag; default h + 1.

level

confidence levels for the pointwise bands.

dof_adjust

apply an n/(n-m) small-sample factor to the Newey-West variance.

Value

an lp_state object: arrays $estimate, $se ((H+1) x K x 3, last dimension high, low, diff = low - high), $bands, $tstat/$pvalue for the difference, $wald (joint test of equality over horizons, per response), the transition $F and $cutoff, and $raw (coefficient array and cross-horizon covariance from the engine) with $contrasts. tidy() returns one row per horizon, response, state and band level.

Details

Timing conventions. timing = "contemporaneous" (default) is the shock-regression form above (observed or external shock \(s_t\), as in lp()). timing = "lagged" replicates the convention of lpirfs::lp_nl: the regressors are lags of \(y\) interacted with the state, with no contemporaneous terms; the horizon-\(h\) response is the coefficient on \(y_{t-1}\) in the equation for \(y_{t+h-1}\) multiplied by column shock of the Cholesky impact matrix of a linear VAR (standard-deviation shock when shock_type = 0, unit own-impact when 1), and the impact response (h = 0) is that column of the impact matrix in both states. Differences to lpirfs: bands here are normal quantiles at level (not a user-supplied multiplier); lpirfs uses Newey-West lag \(h\) for its horizon \(h\) (regression of \(y_{t+h-1}\)), which equals the default \(L=(h-1)+1\) here; lpirfs has no state-specific constants (state_const = FALSE).

Economic intuition. Fiscal and monetary multipliers are often larger in recessions; this estimates state-specific responses without a nonlinear VAR, so the state can change over the horizon without being imposed. The cost is variance: each state uses only the observations weighted by \(F\) or \(1-F\), so effective samples are small and bands wide, and with persistent states the difference test has low power at long horizons. Pitfalls: the calibrated gamma and cutoff are not estimated (AG use \(\gamma=1.5\) and a cutoff so that the low state has about 20% weight, see low_share); a state that is endogenous to the shock beyond one lag contaminates the comparison; with the binary version one state may have very few observations.

References

Auerbach, A. and Gorodnichenko, Y. (2012) Measuring the output responses to fiscal policy. AEJ: Economic Policy; (2013) Fiscal multipliers in recession and expansion.

See also

Other local projections: autoplot.lpm(), compare_lp_var(), lp(), lp_forecast(), lp_joint(), lp_panel(), lp_smooth(), lp_supt(), tidy.lpm()

Examples

fit <- lp_state(
  yraw,
  shock = rate,
  state = infl,
  horizon = 8,
  lags = 2,
  contemp = c(infl, unemp),
  gamma = 3,
  low_share = 0.3
)
fit$estimate[, 3, ]
